content:
The first threat came folded inside a housing petition.

That was what made me angry.

Not the threat itself.

I had been insulted in print often enough to develop standards.

No, what made me angry was that someone had used twenty-seven real tenant signatures as wrapping paper for intimidation.

The petition concerned rent caps in the factory district. The signatures were legitimate. The complaint was legitimate. So was the dried mud on the pages from somebody carrying them through rain.

Tucked between page six and seven was a strip of clean paper.

STOP STANDING BETWEEN NONBENDERS AND THEIR OWN POWER.

Below it:

THE AVATAR CANNOT LOVE US INTO EQUALITY.

I read it twice.

Then a third time.

The clerk beside me asked, “Is something wrong?”

“No.”

A lie.

I folded the note and slipped it into my pocket.

That was another lie, just performed with my hands.

For three hours I said nothing.

I processed the petition. I scheduled witnesses. I corrected a budget total. I told myself the note was political frustration, not a threat. I told myself whoever wrote it had a point buried somewhere beneath the ugliness: the city could not build equality around access to powerful benders, even benevolent ones.

Then I went to lunch and found a second note beneath my bowl.

LEAVE THE AVATAR’S HOUSE OR STOP CLAIMING TO SPEAK FOR US.

My hands went cold.

Toph found me ten minutes later.

She stopped in the doorway of my office.

“Who scared you?”

“I’m not scared.”

“Wrong answer.”

I gave her the notes.

She could not read them.

I read them aloud.

The room went quiet.

Toph’s expression hardened in stages.

“Who touched your desk?”

“I don’t know.”

“Who brought lunch?”

“The stall downstairs.”

“Who carried it up?”

“I did.”

“So somebody came in here.”

“Yes.”

The word tasted different when spoken.

Toph planted both feet.

I could almost feel her listening outward through the building, mapping footsteps, walls, pipes, the vibration of clerks moving in neighboring rooms.

“They’re gone,” she said.

“You can tell?”

“I can tell nobody out there is standing still listening to us.”

That did not mean whoever had left the note was not nearby.

It meant they knew how to disappear into a crowded office.

Aang arrived first because Toph sent a student running for him.

Katara arrived second because Aang had enough sense to send for her before doing anything heroic.

I was angry about both.

“I did not ask for an emergency council.”

Katara closed the office door.

“Someone entered your workspace and left a threat.”

“A note.”

“A threat.”

Aang sat across from me. “We’re not deciding what it means without you.”

That disarmed me more effectively than Katara’s tone.

Toph leaned against the wall.

“I think it means somebody’s an idiot.”

“Useful,” I said.

“I’m here for analysis.”

We read the wording again.

That mattered.

The author did not threaten to hurt me directly. They demanded I leave our household or stop speaking publicly about nonbender rights.

“It could be somebody from the Equal Civic League,” Katara said.

“No.”

Three faces turned toward me.

I shook my head. “Mara would never write this.”

Mara Sen chaired the largest nonbender labor coalition in the city. She had argued with Aang in public, with Toph in louder public, and with me in enough meetings to qualify as a recurring weather pattern.

She also believed in elections, unions, workplace safety, and boring procedural reform.

Toph said, “Doesn’t mean one of her people didn’t.”

“No. But we do not turn a whole rights movement into suspects because someone used their language.”

Aang nodded immediately.

Katara’s jaw tightened.

Then she nodded too.

That mattered.

We spent the afternoon doing the least dramatic thing possible.

We documented everything.

The building supervisor changed the office locks. Clerks logged visitors. The lunch stall confirmed nobody had handled my order after I picked it up, which meant the second note had probably been placed in my office earlier and tucked beneath the bowl after I set it down.

Toph wanted to sleep under my desk.

I told her no.

She said she could disguise herself as a cabinet.

I told her definitely no.

“Coward.”

That evening, Mara came to our house.

She arrived furious.

Not at me.

At the note.

“This is exactly what we do not need,” she said, pacing our kitchen. “Every time some idiot decides intimidation is liberation, every councilman who wants to ignore us gets to point and say, see?”

Toph sat at the table, listening.

“You think it’s one of yours?”

Mara stopped.

“I think nobody belongs to me.”

Toph’s mouth tilted.

Respect.

Mara looked at me. “But yes. There’s a splinter group. Young. Angry. Mostly factory workers who think negotiation is a way powerful people teach everyone else to wait politely.”

“Are they violent?” Katara asked.

“Not as far as I know.”

Aang said, “As far as you know.”

Mara turned toward him.

“Yes, Avatar. That uncertainty is why I am standing in your kitchen helping you.”

Aang held up both hands. “Fair.”

Mara exhaled.

“I disagree with half your approach to this city.”

“Only half?” Toph asked.

“I was being polite.”

“I like her,” Toph announced.

Mara ignored her.

She looked at me again. “But nobody gets to decide you stop being a nonbender because you sleep with benders.”

The sentence struck deeper than the threat had.

That was the wound underneath it.

The notes accused me of betrayal because love had supposedly moved me out of my own category.

As if proximity to power erased where I stood.

As if intimacy were an ideology.

“I worry about that,” I admitted.

Katara looked at me.

I continued before I could retreat.

“I sit at tables other nonbenders don’t get invited to because I know Aang. People answer my letters because my address is public. I can ask Toph whether a building is structurally dangerous and get an answer before inspection forms are processed.”

Toph said, “You also knew us before you slept with us.”

“That doesn’t make the access imaginary.”

“No,” Mara said. “It makes it something you have to account for.”

I looked at her.

“Not apologize for existing,” she added. “Account for.”

There was a difference.

Aang leaned forward. “How?”

Mara’s eyebrows rose.

He did not flinch.

“If my relationship creates access other people don’t have, how do we keep that from becoming policy by bedroom?”

Toph muttered, “That phrase is disgusting.”

“Accurate though,” Katara said.

We spent two hours designing safeguards.

Public logs of policy meetings.

Written conflict-of-interest disclosures.

No private household decisions substituted for formal consultation.

A citizen advisory board with seats selected by neighborhood organizations rather than appointed by Aang.

I hated how much I liked it.

By the time Mara left, the original threats had become evidence in an investigation and an uncomfortable mirror we had chosen not to smash.

The person responsible was identified four days later.

A records messenger named Pell.

Nineteen. Nonbender. Father injured in a bending-driven press accident. Angry enough to become stupid. Frightened enough, when confronted, to confess before Toph finished asking the first question.

He had not planned violence.

That did not erase the intimidation.

I refused to demand prison.

I also refused to call it harmless.

Pell lost his city job, received a restraining order barring him from my office and home, and entered a restorative justice process with the labor coalition only after I agreed.

Mara told him, in front of me, “If you want nonbenders to have power, stop acting like other nonbenders belong to you.”

I could have kissed her.

I did not.

Toph would have made it everyone’s problem.

That night I came home and found the kitchen crowded.

Aang was making dumplings badly.

Katara was fixing them.

Toph was eating filling with her fingers.

Nobody asked whether I wanted to talk about Pell immediately.

Aang nudged a bowl toward me.

Katara touched my shoulder once.

Toph hooked her foot around my ankle beneath the table.

People who stay, I realized, are not always the people who stand between you and danger.

Sometimes they stand beside you while you decide what safety means.

Sometimes they tell you where your own power has become unfair.

Sometimes they refuse to let somebody else define you by who you love.

And sometimes they save you the least ugly dumpling.

Toph stole mine.

Family remained imperfect.

The threat changed the way we moved through the city, but I refused to let it make every choice for us.

That was easier to say than practice.

Aang began glancing at rooftops when we walked. Katara started carrying more water than usual. Toph noticed unfamiliar footsteps before they reached our street and then pretended she had always paid that much attention.

I started checking the latch twice.

The second time was never useful.

One night, I stood with my hand on the door after everyone else had gone to bed.

Toph’s voice came from the hallway. “It’s locked.”

“I know.”

“You checked.”

“I know.”

“So why are you still touching it?”

I let go.

She came to stand beside me, bare feet silent on the wood.

“I hate this,” I said.

“Good.”

I looked at her.

“Would be weird if you liked threats.”

Despite myself, I laughed.

Toph leaned one shoulder against the wall. “You want me to tell you nobody can get in?”

“No.”

“Good, because that would be a lie.”

There it was: comfort, Toph-style.

She continued, “But if somebody tries, they deal with all of us. And the neighbors. And Penga. Penga scares me.”

“Penga is sixteen.”

“Exactly. Terrifying.”

The next morning, the family across the lane brought us steamed buns because they had heard about the threat. A machinist from the eastern district installed a better hinge and refused payment. Two academy students began taking the long route home so they could pass our street.

We had spent months learning that safety could not be built by making one powerful person responsible for everyone.

Apparently neither could love.

People who stayed did not always stand inside the house. Sometimes they lived three doors down and knew how to repair a hinge.
